own_scenes.desc: En otoño de 1966 el impulso lineal del modernismo se había acelerado más allá de lo sostenible y el tiempo se rompía en bucles: el ahora perpetuo o cualquier época sacada a voluntad de unos medios saturados. «Tomorrow Never Knows» y «Tell Me That You Love Me» de James Brown (bucles sobre una grabación en directo, precursora de los breakbeats de la jungle) borraban pasado y futuro en un Ahora eterno. Para McLuhan los jóvenes eran procesadores de datos y había dos niveles de percepción entre quienes nacieron con los medios de masas y quienes no; la televisión convertía el presente en pasado al instante y canibalizaba el pasado. Las series Time Tunnel y Adam Adamant Lives! jugaban con viajes en el tiempo; Beardsley, en el V&A y en la portada de Revolver, sustituyó a lo victoriano; I Was Lord Kitchener’s Valet vendía uniformes antiguos (la casaca de Jagger) y Granny Takes a Trip mezclaba ropa de época y LSD. «Nostalgia del AHORA», había dicho Pauline Boty.

influences.name: Warhol, la Factory y el pop de 1966

refs.q: Something very strange was happening to time in pop culture during autumn 1966
refs.para: Something very strange was happening to time in pop culture during autumn 1966, and ‘Winchester Cathedral’ was only one manifestation of this warp and woof. The unitary drive of modernism had accelerated beyond the point of sustainability. Under this pressure, time was beginning to fragment, from forward motion into a sequence of loops, into either the perpetual now or the historical periods sourced at will by an overloaded media. It was as though the time travel fictionalised by the film version of H. G. Wells’s The Time Machine had come to pass.
refs.chapter: Octubre: Winchester Cathedral: tiempo pasado, presente y futuro

refs.q: Two extraordinary records blew up linear time in their respective quests for a perpetual present.
refs.para: Two extraordinary records blew up linear time in their respective quests for a perpetual present. Placed as the last track on Revolver, the Beatles’ ‘Tomorrow Never Knows’ was heard by millions of listeners, a mass market avant-garde artefact that fused radical technology – in particular the use of tape loops, backwards tapes and Leslie speakers – with the most explicit evocation yet in popular culture of mystical transcendence. Its form reflected the circularity of the lyrics, which faded on the end of the beginning.
refs.chapter: Octubre: Winchester Cathedral: tiempo pasado, presente y futuro

refs.q: ‘Nostalgia for NOW’ was a perfect slogan for the mid-sixties: grasp the moment and it had gone.
refs.para: In the November 1962 issue of Scene, the painter Pauline Boty had talked about the relationship of past and present. As she moved towards pop art, Boty defined her aesthetic as ‘Nostalgia for NOW’: ‘People have this kind of nostalgia for Victoriana and we have a nostalgia for things that are now … it’s almost like painting mythology, only a present day mythology – film stars etc.’ ‘Nostalgia for NOW’ was a perfect slogan for the mid-sixties: grasp the moment and it had gone.
